title: Detection of Digital Certificates
summary: This strategy detects the Digital Certificates search technique, in which an adversary reviews certificate records to learn about victim infrastructure, including host names, subdomains, mail servers, and internal naming conventions. It matters because certificate transparency logs are public by design, so this reconnaissance leaves no trace on victim systems and is nearly impossible to block; the practical value is knowing when your own naming data is being harvested and when a suspicious certificate appears for one of your domains. Detection relies on monitoring certificate transparency feeds for your domain names, watching for certificates issued by unexpected authorities, and correlating newly seen host names with subsequent authentication or scan activity. It fails when the organisation has no domain inventory, so legitimate certificates for partner and regional names generate noise.

beginner.definition: This detection watches public certificate records for signs that your domain names are being studied. A digital certificate is a small file that proves a website is really who it claims to be. Anyone can read the public list of certificates, so this search is legal and quiet.
beginner.whyItMatters: Certificates reveal host names that you may never have published, such as internal tools and test systems. An attacker can use those names to plan a targeted attack. Because the record is public, you cannot stop the search. You can only watch what appears in it. That helps you find exposure you did not know you had.
howItWorks: The rule learns which domains the organisation owns and monitors a public certificate log.
New certificate records for those domains are collected as they are published.
Each record is checked for the issuing authority and the names it covers.
A certificate issued by an unexpected authority, or covering lookalike names, raises interest.
Newly seen host names are added to an inventory list for further review.
Analysts confirm whether the certificate belongs to the organisation before acting.
beginner.example: Think of a public library notice board. Anyone may read the notices, and reading them is not a crime. The danger is what you put on the board: a notice that says which office is empty at night. Certificate logs are that notice board. You cannot stop people reading, so you must choose carefully what the board reveals and watch for forged notices.
takeaways: Public certificate logs expose host names without giving the attacker any contact with your systems.
Unexpected issuers or lookalike names for your domains are the events worth alerting on.
An accurate domain inventory is the foundation of this detection.

objectives: Explain what a digital certificate is and why certificate logs are public
Describe how certificate records leak host names useful for reconnaissance
Configure monitoring of certificate transparency records for owned domains
Distinguish a legitimate new certificate from one issued by an unexpected authority
Correlate a newly observed host name with later authentication or scan events
dataSources: Certificate transparency log monitoring feeds filtered to organisation owned domain names
Passive DNS records showing resolution of newly observed certificate host names
Public certificate authority issuance records for lookalike and typosquat domains
External attack surface monitoring inventory of owned domains and subdomains
Endpoint certificate store inventory from operating system and browser trust stores
logic: The pattern is certificate data that touches your namespaces in ways you did not authorise: a certificate for an owned or lookalike domain issued by an authority you do not use, a sudden block of certificates enumerating many of your subdomains from one requester, or a newly appearing internal style host name that then resolves and receives authentication traffic. The fields to correlate are the domain name, the issuing authority, the issuance timestamp, the certificate subject alternative names, and later DNS or authentication events for those names. Benign cases are ordinary renewals for known public services, certificates for regional or partner domains that operations teams manage, and marketing sites stood up by agencies. The malicious case is bulk enumeration of subdomains, wildcard certificates for lookalike names, and issuers that never appear in your change process.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Unexpected Certificate Issued For Owned Domain
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   category: certificate_transparency
# detection:
#   selection:
#     domain|endswith: '.example[.]com'
#   filter:
#     issuer|contains:
#       - 'ApprovedCorporateCA'
#   condition: selection and not filter
# level: medium
falsePositives: Marketing or regional teams issuing certificates for new public domains through an agency
Automated certificate renewal by a content delivery network using a different authority than expected
Partner or subsidiary domains that are owned by the business but not listed in the domain inventory
Test and sandbox domains created by developers with short lived free certificates
tuningNotes: Maintain an authoritative domain and subdomain inventory and an approved issuer list before enabling alerts, then filter on those two dimensions rather than on individual certificate names. Add volume thresholds so that a single unexpected certificate is informational while a burst of issuances from one requester alerts. Enrich with passive DNS to see whether the new name resolves to your infrastructure or elsewhere. Narrowing to owned domains loses visibility of typosquatting and brand abuse, so keep a separate lower severity feed for lookalike names and review it weekly.
